1H (Number Theory)

Words: 148 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 148
1H OurBigBook.com
Let g generate the cyclic group of nonzero residues, whose order p−1=22n is a power of two. Write a=gj. Its multiplicative order is (p−1)/gcd(j,p−1), so it is a primitive root precisely when j is odd. The quadratic residues are exactly the even powers of g. Thus the primitive roots are precisely the quadratic nonresidues, with nonzero residue classes understood.
For n≥1, p≡1(mod4), so quadratic reciprocity gives (7/p)=(p/7). Since 23≡1(mod7) and 2n alternates between 1 and 2 modulo three, p is respectively 3 or 5 modulo seven. The nonzero squares modulo seven are 1,2,4. Consequently (7/p)=−1, and
7 is a primitive root modulo every Fermat prime 22n+1 with n≥1.​
(1)
There is a genuine endpoint exception if the printed form permits n=0: then p=3 and 7≡1(mod3), which has order one and is not primitive. The first equivalence remains true for p=3, but the final assertion requires excluding that prime.

i OurBigBook.com
The Liouville approximation theorem states that if α is a real irrational algebraic number of degree d, there is a constant C(α)>0 such that, for all integers p,q with q=0,
​α−qp​​≥∣q∣dC(α)​.​
(2)
Reduction of the fraction is not necessary: an unreduced denominator only weakens this bound. More generally the same type of bound holds for an algebraic number of degree d whenever p/q=α. The exception is essential for a rational α, since an exact rational representation gives zero error. A rational number of degree one obeys the bound directly: if α=a/b in lowest terms and p/q=α, then ∣α−p/q∣=∣aq−bp∣/(∣bq∣)≥1/(∣bq∣).

ii OurBigBook.com
Set r=p/q. If r∈/[1,2], then ∣2​−r∣≥2​−1>1/4≥1/(4q2). If 1≤r≤2, irrationality of the square root of two implies that the integer 2q2−p2 is nonzero. Factoring a difference of squares therefore gives
​2​−qp​​=q2(2​+p/q)∣2q2−p2∣​≥q2(2​+2)1​>4q21​.
(3)
Thus the requested bound holds for every integer p and every nonzero integer q, without using the Liouville approximation theorem. For completeness, irrationality follows because p2=2q2 in lowest terms would make p even and then q even, contradicting coprimality.

3G (Geometry of Group Actions)

Words: 110 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 110
3G OurBigBook.com
Use the curvature-minus-one Poincare disc model, whose Riemannian metric is
ds2=(1−x2−y2)24(dx2+dy2)​.
(4)
Its geodesics are Euclidean diameters and arcs of circles meeting the boundary circle orthogonally. The hyperbolic area of a measurable region D is
Area(D)=∫D​(1−x2−y2)24​dxdy.
(5)
An isometry can move the center of a circle to the origin. Its hyperbolic radius r and Euclidean radius ρ then satisfy r=∫0ρ​2du/(1−u2)=2artanhρ, so ρ=tanh(r/2). Integrating the area element of a surface in polar coordinates yields
A(r)=∫02π​∫0ρ​(1−u2)24u​dudθ=1−ρ24πρ2​=2π(coshr−1)​.
(6)
Integrating the line element around the circle gives
C(r)=1−ρ24πρ​=2πsinhr​,A′(r)=2πsinhr=C(r).
(7)
A geometric definition of Pi valid in this geometry is
π=r↓0lim​2rC(r)​=r↓0lim​r2A(r)​.​
(8)
Indeed sinhr=r+O(r3) and coshr=1+r2/2+O(r4). The circumference-to-diameter ratio at a fixed positive radius is not constant, so the limiting qualification is necessary.

4J (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 131 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 131
4J OurBigBook.com
A binary linear code of length n is a vector subspace C⊆F2n​. The Hamming weight of a word counts its nonzero coordinates, and the code weight is w(C)=min0=c∈C​wt(c); for a linear code this equals its minimum distance. One may assign infinite minimum weight to the zero code when needed.
For length-n codes with C2​⊆C1​, the bar product of binary linear codes is
C1​∣C2​={(u,u+v):u∈C1​, v∈C2​}⊆F22n​.
(9)
It is a linear code because this map from C1​⊕C2​ is linear and injective. For a nonzero codeword, if v=0 then u=0 and its weight is 2wt(u)≥2w(C1​). If v=0, every nonzero coordinate of v makes exactly one of the corresponding coordinates of u,u+v nonzero; hence
wt(u)+wt(u+v)≥wt(v)≥w(C2​).
(10)
Taking the minimum gives
w(C1​∣C2​)≥min{2w(C1​),w(C2​)}.​
(11)
In fact equality holds when the codes are nonzero: minimum-weight words (u,u) and (0,v) attain the two candidate weights.

5I (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 367 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 367
5I OurBigBook.com
Each scan() command reads a numeric vector from the entered data: the first creates the nine counts, and the second their nine predictor values. The last command fits a generalized linear model with the Poisson distribution and its default log link, including an intercept, then prints a summary. Thus the model is independent counts with means μj​ satisfying
logμj​=b0​+b1​ij​,μ​j​=exp(1.363+0.3106ij​).
(12)
The coefficients are maximum-likelihood estimates, and the reported standard errors come from the inverse fitted Fisher information matrix. Increasing the predictor by one multiplies the fitted mean by e0.3106≃1.364, about a 36.4% increase. The intercept corresponds to a mean e1.363≃3.91 at predictor zero, outside the observed range. Approximate coefficient-to-standard-error ratios are 6.17 and 8.13; the slope is strongly different from zero under the assumed model. A 95% Wald confidence interval for the slope is about [0.236,0.385], or [1.266,1.470] for the multiplicative change.
The deviance is twice the log-likelihood advantage of the saturated model over the fitted model. For these counts it is
D=2∑j=19​[nj​logμ​j​nj​​−(nj​−μ​j​)],
(13)
with the logarithmic term interpreted as zero when a count is zero. The saturated model has nine freely fitted means; the fitted model has two independent regression coefficients, so the residual degrees of freedom are 9−2=7.
Under an adequate Poisson model and the usual large-sample approximation, D is compared with χ72​. The reported 13.218 is rather large relative to seven, but below the 5% upper critical value about 14.07; its approximate upper-tail probability is 0.067. Thus there is some indication of lack of fit or overdispersion, but not a rejection at the 5% level on this diagnostic. The deviance-to-d.f. ratio is about 1.89; it does not by itself prove an overdispersed model, and the chi-square approximation is imperfect for small counts.
There is one inconsistency in the supplied numerical output. Independently solving the Poisson score equations for the displayed nine counts gives b0​=1.363454, b1​=0.310563 and deviance 13.217971, agreeing with the printed estimates and deviance. But [XTdiag(μ​)X]−1 gives standard errors approximately 0.221295 and 0.030850. In particular the printed slope standard error 0.0382 is not the standard Poisson-model value for these data. The interpretations above describe the supplied numbers; the directly recomputed slope ratio is 10.07 and its normal-approximation 95% interval is about [0.2501,0.3710]. The conclusion of a strong increasing trend is unchanged.

Apply the formal infinitesimal generator to the molecule count: its increment is +1 at rate λ and −2 at rate βx2. Thus the exact first-moment identity for the specified generator is
dtd​⟨x⟩=λ−2β⟨x2⟩=λ−2β(⟨x⟩2+Varx).​
(14)
Neglecting fluctuations gives the mean-field approximation m˙=λ−2βm2, so the positive steady mean is
m=⟨x⟩≃λ/(2β)​.​
(15)
There is a physical boundary qualification: the printed loss propensity is positive at x=1 and would produce a negative molecule count. Consequently it does not by itself define a molecule-count chain on all nonnegative integers. If losses are forbidden below two, the exact loss moment becomes 2βE[x21{x≥2}​]; a mass-action two-molecule propensity instead uses x(x−1). The calculation requested here uses the printed formal generator and its large-copy-number approximation, where such boundary corrections are negligible.

H=dlogmdlogJ−​​−dlogmdlogJ+​​=2,τ=Jm​=λm​=2βm1​.​
(16)
Flux-weighting the magnitudes of the reaction steps, one for production and two for loss, gives
⟨r⟩=J+​+J−​J+​⋅1+J−​⋅2​=23​.​
(17)
This is an average over molecular fluxes, as requested, not an average over reaction-event counts; those are different when a reaction removes two molecules at once.

η=m2Varx​=Hm⟨r⟩​.​

B=λ⋅12+βm2⋅(−2)2=3λ.
(19)
Stationarity of the variance gives 2aVarx=B. Using λ=2βm2 therefore yields
Varx=43m​,η=4m3​=4⟨x⟩3​.​

7B (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 206 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 206
7B OurBigBook.com
A fixed point x0​ is Lyapunov stable if for every ε>0 there is δ>0 such that solutions starting within δ of x0​ stay within ε for all forward times. It has quasi-asymptotic stability if some neighborhood of x0​ consists of initial points whose solutions converge to x0​. Asymptotic stability requires both properties.
Choose the Lyapunov function
V(x,y)=3x6​+y2.​
(21)
It vanishes only at the origin, is positive elsewhere, and has compact sublevel sets. The vector field is polynomial, hence locally Lipschitz. Along a solution,
V˙=2x5(−y−x3)+2yx5=−2x8≤0.
(22)
A small sublevel set is forward invariant and can be fitted inside any prescribed neighborhood, proving Lyapunov stability; boundedness also prevents finite-time escape.
For attraction, a bounded forward solution has a nonempty compact limit set, and V decreases to a limit. Every point in that limit set has that same V value. Continuous dependence of solutions makes the limit set forward invariant, so V˙=0 along every trajectory in it. Such a trajectory must have x=0 at all times. But then x˙=−y, forcing y=0. Thus the only possible limit point is the origin, and every solution converges there. This verifies the invariant-set condition behind the LaSalle invariance principle, rather than incorrectly treating V˙ as strictly negative at every nonzero point. The origin is therefore asymptotically stable, indeed globally attracting.

8A (Further Complex Methods)

Words: 197 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 197
8A OurBigBook.com
Fix a Hankel contour with a positive-radius circle around zero and a branch −π<argt<π, traversing the lower bank inwards and the upper bank outwards. Write its numerator as I(z)=∫H​tz−1etdt. For fixed circle radius, I is an entire function of z: the finite contour pieces avoid zero, and the tails converge uniformly on compact z sets by exponential decay, also after differentiation with respect to z.
At z=−n, the two straight-bank contributions cancel because t−n−1et is single-valued. The remaining circle is positively oriented, so the residue theorem and the exponential series give
I(−n)=2πiRest=0​(t−n−1et)=n!2πi​.
(23)
Since sin(πz)=(−1)nπ(z+n)+O((z+n)3), the quotient has the simple pole
Resz=−n​Γ(z)=n!(−1)n​,n≥0.​
(24)
For cancellation of positive-integer gamma singularities on a Hankel contour, at a positive integer n, the integrand tn−1et is entire and its bank contributions again cancel; its circular integral is zero. Hence I(n)=0. The numerator is analytic near n, while the denominator has a simple zero with nonzero derivative. Factoring I(z)=(z−n)J(z) therefore cancels that zero, proving there is no pole at a positive integer using only this representation. Cancellation of the numerator, not merely the zero of the sine, decides the issue. One can also shrink the contour for ℜz>0, obtaining I(z)=2isin(πz)∫0∞​uz−1e−udu and hence the finite value (n−1)!.

Words: 187
9C OurBigBook.com
The components in Euler equations for a torque-free rigid body are evaluated in the body-fixed principal-axis frame, with Li​=Ii​ωi​. In an inertial space frame the angular momentum vector is constant; its components in the rotating body frame need not be.
Assume Ω=0 and distinct positive principal moments of inertia. Write ω=(Ω+δ1​,δ2​,δ3​). To first order,
δ˙1​=0,δ˙2​=I2​I3​−I1​​Ωδ3​,δ˙3​=I3​I1​−I2​​Ωδ2​,
(25)
so
δ¨2​=Ω2I2​I3​(I3​−I1​)(I1​−I2​)​δ2​.
(26)
The coefficient is positive when I1​ lies between the other moments, giving an exponentially growing mode and instability. When I1​ is an extreme moment, it is negative and the transverse perturbations oscillate.
To establish actual nonlinear Lyapunov stability in the latter case, use the conserved kinetic energy E=21​∑Ij​ωj2​ and squared angular momentum L2=∑Ij2​ωj2​. Their combination is
L2−2I1​E=I2​(I2​−I1​)ω22​+I3​(I3​−I1​)ω32​.
(27)
For an extreme I1​ its two coefficients have the same sign. Conservation controls both transverse components by their initially small values, while conservation of E controls ω12​ near Ω2. Continuity preserves its initial sign for sufficiently small perturbations. Thus nonzero steady rotation is stable exactly about the largest or smallest principal moment, the intermediate axis theorem. It is not asymptotically stable, since energy is conserved. If Ω=0, energy makes the zero angular-velocity state stable for every ordering; the nonzero-rotation assumption is essential to the stated equivalence.

∫0R​4πr3P′(r)dr=[4πr3P]0R​−3∫0R​4πr2Pdr=−3⟨P⟩V.

The other side is −∫0R​4πGm(r)ρ(r)rdr=−∫0M​Gm/r(m)dm. Building the star one shell at a time identifies this as its negative gravitational potential energy Egrav​. Therefore

Within the prescribed uniform-density approximation, n=3M/(4πmp​R3). Treating the given approximate pressure coefficient as one, the degeneracy pressure and specified kinetic-energy relation give
Ekin​=23​me​h2​n5/334πR3​=R2α​,α=23​me​h2​(4π3​)2/3(mp​M​)5/3.
(30)
For a uniform sphere, m(r)=M(r/R)3, so shell assembly gives
Egrav​=−∫0R​rGm(r)​dm(r)=−5R3GM2​.

Etotal​(R)=R2α​−Rβ​,β=53​GM2.​

Expansion beyond this radius raises the energy, while strong compression costs positive energy growing as R−2, faster than the attractive R−1 term. This explains radial stability of the model white dwarf. The numerical coefficient in α inherits the approximate pressure law; a relativistic degeneracy law would change this stability argument.

Solution

Words: 78
i OurBigBook.com
The Baire category theorem says that in a nonempty complete metric space, a countable intersection of open dense subsets is dense. Equivalently, such a space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets: a set is nowhere dense when the interior of its closure is empty. Indeed the complements of those closures are open dense; their intersection is dense and in particular nonempty, so a countable union of the original sets cannot exhaust the space. The same argument shows that the complement of such a union is dense.

ii OurBigBook.com
First interpret the decimal expansions as fractional expansions 0.d1​d2​⋯, with every dj​∈{4,5}. The resulting set X0​ is compact: a diagonal subsequence argument selects successively stabilized digits from any sequence in X0​, and the tail bound ∑j>m​9⋅10−j=10−m proves convergence to the corresponding expansion.
It has empty interior. At level m its points lie in 2m decimal intervals, each of length 10−m, whose total length is (1/5)m. An interval of positive length could not lie in all these covers. Thus X0​ is closed and nowhere dense. Each translate X0​+q is also nowhere dense, and the rational numbers are countable. The Baire category theorem applied to R yields
R∖q∈Q⋃​(X0​+q)=∅.​
(33)
Any point in this complement has the required property. If the printed description also permits integer digits before the decimal point, there are only countably many such integer parts, and negative expansions merely add reflected translates. This makes X a countable union of translates or reflections of X0​. The same countable-union argument therefore still proves that some real t cannot be written as x+q.

Solution

Words: 614
12J OurBigBook.com
A linear-feedback shift register of length d has binary state (xr​,…,xr+d−1​) and update
f(v0​,…,vd−1​)=(v1​,…,vd−1​,∑j=0d−1​aj​vj​).
(34)
Its output obeys xr+d​=∑j=0d−1​aj​xr+j​ over F2​. Since the state space is finite, its trajectory consists of a transient of length M followed by a cycle of length N≥1, and the output satisfies xr+N​=xr​ for r≥M.
If the trajectory never reaches zero, all its M+N distinct transient and cyclic states are nonzero; hence M+N≤2d−1. If it reaches zero, let M be its first zero-state time. The vectors v,fv,…,fM−1v are linearly independent: in a dependence, apply fM−1−j where j is the smallest index with a nonzero coefficient; every later term vanishes and the remaining term is fM−1v=0. Therefore M≤d. The zero cycle has N=1, and d+1≤2d−1 for d≥2. This proves the requested bound for all d≥2, and for every invertible register.
The unrestricted printed assertion has one exception: at d=1, the zero-feedback register with initial state one outputs 1,0,0,…. It requires M≥1,N≥1, so M+N≥2>21−1. The universally valid finite-state bound is M+N≤2d. A register with feedback from its oldest bit is invertible, in which case a nonzero state never reaches zero and the sharper bound holds already with M=0.
To recover an unknown register from a known plaintext/ciphertext keystream, the Berlekamp-Massey algorithm finds a shortest linear recurrence consistent with the observed bits. Use a connection polynomial C(z)=1+∑j=1L​Cj​zj, so the recurrence discrepancy at index r is δ=xr​+∑j=1L​Cj​xr−j​. Initialize C=B=1,L=0,b=1,m=1. Process the bits in order. If δ=0, increment m. If δ=0, save T=C and replace
C⟵C+(δ/b)zmB.
(35)
If 2L≤r, also replace L by r+1−L, set B=T,b=δ,m=1; otherwise retain L,B,b and increment m. Arithmetic is binary, so every nonzero discrepancy equals one. The stored polynomial B last failed at an earlier index with discrepancy b; its shifted contribution cancels the new failure without changing previous successful discrepancies.
Here is the minimum recurrence length after a new discrepancy argument behind the update, not just its name. Suppose a span-L recurrence C succeeds through index r−1 but fails at r. If another polynomial D of span L′ succeeded through r and L+L′≤r, compute the convolution (CD)x at r in two ways. Applying D first gives zero, since all indices r−j used by C lie at least at L′. Applying C first gives its nonzero discrepancy at r, since its earlier discrepancies used by D vanish and D0​=1. This contradiction proves L′≥r+1−L. The shifted-polynomial update attains the larger of the existing minimum length and this new lower bound; induction therefore gives the shortest recurrence for every prefix. Once at least twice the true linear complexity has been observed, this recurrence determines the whole stream: the difference from a true degree-d recurrent stream satisfies a recurrence of degree at most d+L, and a prefix of that many zeros forces every later value to be zero. Without any bound on complexity, a finite observed prefix cannot exclude a longer register that diverges later; the breaking claim uses the finite-register hypothesis and adequate known data.
Finally each of the three input streams is eventually periodic. Let M be the maximum of their transient lengths and N a common multiple of their periods. Their joint triple, and hence the bit chosen by the specified rule, repeats after N once r≥M. Therefore
kr+M+N​=kr+M​(r≥0).
(36)
This itself is a linear recurrence of length M+N, so it constructs a linear-feedback shift register producing the selected stream from its first M+N bits. No closure theorem is being assumed: eventual periodicity and this explicit recurrence prove the combined stream is also an LFSR stream, even though the combining rule is nonlinear in its three inputs.

Let the three orbit points be a<b<c. Up to reflection of the interval, their images are F(a)=b,F(b)=c,F(c)=a. Set I=[a,b] and J=[b,c]. Continuity and the intermediate value theorem imply the covering relations
F(I)⊇J,F(J)⊇I∪J.
(46)
We first prove the needed interval-covering principle using the permitted pullback fact. If a cyclic list of closed intervals I0​,…,In−1​,In​=I0​ obeys F(Ij​)⊇Ij+1​, pull back successively from the end to obtain a closed interval K⊆I0​ with Fn(K)=I0​ and Fj(K)⊆Ij​. Since Fn(K)⊇K, the intermediate value theorem gives a fixed point of Fn in K: choose preimages of the two endpoints of K, which give opposite weak signs of Fn(x)−x, irrespective of their order. This point realizes the cyclic itinerary.
For n≥2, use the word IJn−1. It obeys the covering relations and therefore yields a point with period dividing n. A point away from the shared endpoint b has an unambiguous itinerary, and this word has exactly one I per cycle; it cannot be a repetition of a shorter word. Its least period is consequently n. If an orbit touches b, it is the original three-cycle. That realizes the case n=3 itself. It cannot realize any of the other words: for n not divisible by three it is not fixed by Fn, and for a multiple of three larger than three it visits a∈I∖J more than once, contradicting the itinerary. Thus the construction works for every n≥2. For n=1, F(J)⊇J and the same fixed-point argument gives a fixed point. This proves period three implies all periods: there is an orbit of every positive least period.
For the two five-cycles forced by a three-cycle, use the two cyclic words IJJJJ and IJIJJ. Both are admissible. Their points cannot be endpoints from the three-cycle, and because five is prime and the words use both intervals, each has least period five. Their itineraries have respectively one and two visits to the interior of I; cyclically shifting the starting point cannot change this count. Hence they give at least two distinct period-five orbits.

The inductive definition of ordinal addition is
α+0=α,α+(β+1)=(α+β)+1,α+λ=supβ<λ​(α+β)
(55)
for nonzero limit ordinals λ. The synthetic definition is the order type of a disjoint copy of α followed by a disjoint copy of β, retaining the order within each block and declaring every element of the first block smaller than every element of the second.
These are equivalent by transfinite induction in the second argument. An empty second block leaves α; a successor block appends one final point; and a limit block is the increasing union of its proper initial blocks, whose order types have the indicated supremum. Thus the synthetic construction satisfies exactly the inductive recursion, which determines the operation uniquely. It is not commutative: 1+ω=ω, whereas ω+1>ω.

First suppose G is 3-connected and noncomplete, and write Δ=Δ(G). There is an induced path a,v,b with a,b nonadjacent: otherwise the first three vertices of any shortest path between nonadjacent vertices would contradict that assertion. Since G is 3-connected, G−{a,b} is a connected graph. Choose a spanning tree of that graph rooted at v. Color a,b first with the same color, then color the other vertices in reverse tree order, leaving v last. Every vertex except v has its tree parent uncolored and thus at most Δ−1 previously colored neighbors. At v, the two neighbors a,b share a color, so again at most Δ−1 colors are forbidden. This constructs a proper Δ-coloring and proves Brooks' bound for 3-connected noncomplete graphs. A complete graph is exactly the excluded case; a 3-connected graph cannot be an odd cycle.
For the partition claim, assume d1​,d2​ are nonnegative integers with d1​+d2​=Δ−1. Minimize
Φ=d2​e(G[V1​])+d1​e(G[V2​]).
(57)
If a vertex in V1​ has internal degree a≥d1​+1, its degree b into V2​ is at most d2​. Moving it to V2​ changes Φ by d1​b−d2​a≤−d2​, contradicting minimality when d2​>0. The analogous move handles a violation in V2​ when d1​>0. For a zero coefficient, break ties among minimizers by minimizing the total number of internal edges. If d2​=0<d1​, minimality of Φ=d1​e(G[V2​]) ensures V2​ is independent; a violating vertex in V1​ has all its Δ=d1​+1 neighbors in V1​ and no neighbor in V2​, so moving it reduces the tie-break quantity without increasing Φ. The reversed argument handles d1​=0. If both are zero then Δ=1, and the graph is a union of isolated vertices and edges, admitting two independent parts. Thus
Δ(G[Vi​])≤di​(i=1,2).​
(58)
For Δ≥5, put d1​=3,d2​=Δ−4. A maximum-degree-three graph containing no K4​ is 3-colorable. Here is why the previously proved 3-connected case suffices: connected graphs of degree at most two are paths or cycles and use at most three colors. Split a larger graph at cut vertices and permute colors when gluing. In a 2-connected cubic graph with a two-vertex cut {u,v}, a cut edge uv gives colorings of the sides glued with their distinct endpoint colors. If u,v are nonadjacent, the cut components have positive numbers of edges to both endpoints and the total endpoint degrees are at most three. There are at most three components. With three components, adding uv to each side preserves maximum degree three and gives the endpoints degree two. No new K4​ is created, so induction supplies side colorings with distinct endpoint colors, which can be permuted to agree. With two components, the components incident twice to u and twice to v either agree or differ. If they differ, adding uv to each side preserves maximum degree three; each augmented side is smaller and cannot be K4​, because one endpoint then has degree only two, so induction gives distinct-endpoint colorings. If they agree, call the side with only one edge from each endpoint the small side. Any coloring of the other side can be matched on it: for equal endpoint colors, contract u,v in the small side (the merged vertex has degree at most two); for distinct colors add uv (the endpoints again have degree two). Induction applies in both cases. A 2-connected graph with no two-vertex cut is 3-connected and was handled above. This proves the needed subcubic coloring fact without quoting the unproved full theorem.
Use three colors on V1​ and at most d2​+1=Δ−3 fresh colors on V2​, by greedy coloring. This gives χ(G)≤Δ. More usefully, repeatedly remove degree-at-most-three parts: the partition supplies a four-degree reduction for a cost of three colors. If f(Δ)=43​Δ+23​, then 3+f(Δ−4)=f(Δ). Induction in Δ, with the remaining part still K4​-free, gives
χ(G)≤43​Δ(G)+23​.​
(59)
The base cases Δ=0,1,2,3 use respectively 1,2,3,3 colors, within this bound; at Δ=4, Brooks' theorem would give four, but the same partition with (3,0) gives a 3-colorable part and an independent part, hence four. Thus the induction requires no unproved general Brooks theorem.

A linear operator between Banach spaces is a compact operator when it maps the unit ball into a relatively compact set, equivalently when every bounded sequence of inputs has an image subsequence converging in norm. Such an operator is bounded. For a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space, the resolvent set consists of the complex λ for which T−λI is bijective with bounded inverse; its complement is the spectrum. The point spectrum consists of those λ for which T−λI has a nonzero kernel, namely the eigenvalues.
On a Hilbert space, T is self-adjoint if T=T∗, or equivalently ⟨Tx,y⟩=⟨x,Ty⟩ for all vectors. The given prescription extends uniquely to
Tx=∑j≥1​jxj​​ej​,x=∑j​xj​ej​.

It is bounded with norm one. The real diagonal entries prove self-adjointness by the inner-product identity. Define the finite-rank truncation Tm​x=∑j≤m​xj​ej​/j. Then ∥T−Tm​∥=1/(m+1)→0. To see compactness directly, extract successively convergent subsequences of the finitely many first coordinates from a bounded input sequence; the uniform tail bound just displayed makes the resulting image subsequence Cauchy. Hence T is compact and self-adjoint.
Each 1/j is an eigenvalue with eigenspace Cej​. If Tx=λx, each coordinate satisfies (1/j−λ)xj​=0, so there are no other eigenvalues; in particular zero is not an eigenvalue. But ∥Tej​∥=1/j→0, which contradicts a bounded inverse at zero. Thus zero is in the spectrum.
For λ∈/{0,1,1/2,1/3,…}, its distance from this closed set is positive. The diagonal formula
(T−λI)−1y=∑j≥1​1/j−λyj​​ej​
(74)
then defines a bounded inverse. This proves the complete description

23H (Riemann Surfaces)

Words: 384 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 384
23H OurBigBook.com
A function element is a pair (f,D) where D is a nonempty disk and f is holomorphic there; the germ at its center captures its local information. Elements continue one another when their functions agree on an overlapping connected neighborhood. A complete analytic function is a maximal collection reachable from one element by chains of analytic continuation, including all further continuations of its members.
If fn=p in the initial disk, the identity theorem propagates this identity across every overlapping disk in a continuation chain. Induction along the chain proves every element of the complete analytic function also satisfies f​n=p.
Put F(z,w)=wn−p(z). Its gradient is (−p′(z),nwn−1). At a point of the curve with w=0, the second entry is nonzero; at w=0, the root of p is simple and the first entry is nonzero. Thus the holomorphic implicit function theorem supplies charts. Its precise local statement is that a holomorphic equation with nonzero derivative in one variable can locally be solved uniquely and holomorphically for that variable as a function of the other. For w=0, use z as coordinate and write w=w(z); at a simple root use w as coordinate and write z=z(w). The transition maps are holomorphic with nonzero derivatives, giving a Riemann surface. The two projections are holomorphic because they are holomorphic expressions in either kind of chart.
Away from the zeros of p, the projection onto z is an unramified n-sheeted covering. A germ of a root corresponds to (z,f(z)) and its analytic continuations follow this covering. Near a simple root, z−z0​ is a nonzero analytic factor times wn; a circuit about z0​ cyclically permutes all n branches. For nonconstant square-free p, these circuits connect all sheets. Hence the germ surface S(F) is the curve with the points over the roots removed, and C is its branched completion obtained by adding those ramification points. An ordinary function element in the variable z cannot include such a point: the zero order of a holomorphic nth power is divisible by n, whereas p has zero order one. If a convention already includes these branch points in the Riemann surface of a multivalued function, that completed surface is C itself. For a nonzero constant p, the curve has n separate components, and the chosen element determines just one of them. The identically zero polynomial is excluded by the non-singularity premise.

A renewal process counts arrivals N(t)=max{j:Aj​≤t}, where A0​=0,Aj​=S1​+⋯+Sj​ and the holding times are independent, identically distributed positive random variables. Their sum tends to infinity almost surely, so the count is finite on bounded time intervals. Use N(s)=Xs​ in the question's notation. The index J=N(s)+1=min{j:Aj​>s} is a stopping index for the holding-time sequence. Conditional on J=j and the first j holding times, every later Sj+k​ retains its original probability distribution. Summing over j proves
P(Tn​>t)=P(S1​>t)(n≥2).​
(83)
The straddling time T1​=SJ​ is different. Let F(t)=P(S1​>t) and let U be the renewal measure U(B)=∑j≥0​P(Aj​∈B). Independence of the next holding time from its start gives
P(T1​>t)=∫[0,s]​F(max(t,s−u))U(du),1=∫[0,s]​F(s−u)U(du).
(84)
For two numbers in [0,1], their minimum is at least their product. Since F(max(t,a))=min(F(t),F(a)), subtracting F(t) times the second integral proves
P(T1​>t)≥P(S1​>t).​
(85)
These formulae handle holding-time atoms with the stated renewal convention Aj​≤s<Aj+1​; sums may be interchanged by nonnegativity.
For rate-λ exponentials, the renewal process is Poisson. The elapsed age Bs​=s−AN(s)​ has probability distribution min(E,s) with E∼Exp(λ): for 0≤b<s, P(Bs​>b) is the probability of no arrivals in (s−b,s], namely e−λb, with an atom e−λs at s. The forward residual Rs​ is an independent rate-λ exponential by independent future increments. Thus T1​=Bs​+Rs​. Conditioning on the age gives the exact survival law
P(T1​>t)=e−λt[1+λmin(s,t)],t≥0.​
(86)
For s,t>0 the extra term is strictly positive, proving strict inequality. For fixed t and s→∞, the limit is e−λt(1+λt), which equals the survival probability of the sum of two independent rate-λ exponentials. This is the finite-time form of the stochastic length bias of a renewal interval.

A time-homogeneous Markov decision process specifies a state space, admissible actions at each state, an action-dependent transition kernel and one-step reward, with neither kernel nor reward depending on time. A policy chooses actions using the observed history. The positive programming case has nonnegative rewards and maximizes expected undiscounted total reward, allowing infinite values; its finite-horizon values increase to the infinite-horizon supremum under the appropriate approximation argument.
Here let τB​ be the absorption time of the underlying simple random walk at 0,N. Every admissible stopping time T is at most τB​. The reward is bounded by Rmax​=maxj​r(j), and Ei​τB​=i(N−i), as follows by solving hi​=1+(hi−1​+hi+1​)/2 with zero endpoint values. In particular absorption is almost surely finite. Truncating any policy at T∧n changes its reward expectation by at most 2Rmax​Pi​(τB​>n)≤2Rmax​i(N−i)/n. Since the truncated policy is allowed in the n-step problem,
Vn​(i)≤V(i)≤Vn​(i)+2Rmax​Pi​(τB​>n).
(98)
This proves Vn​→V, even uniformly on the finite state space.
The finite-horizon recursion starts with V0​=r, fixes the endpoint rewards and has
Vn+1​(i)=max{r(i),21​[Vn​(i−1)+Vn​(i+1)]}.
(99)
Taking limits shows V≥r and 2V(i)≥V(i−1)+V(i+1), so V is discretely concave. If W is any concave function majorizing r, induction in this same recursion gives Vn​≤W, and hence V≤W. Therefore V is the smallest concave majorant of the rewards. At a point where V(i)>r(i) the recursion forces equality with the neighboring average; the value graph is linear through each consecutive continuation region.
An optimal policy stops upon first entering the contact set {i:V(i)=r(i)} and continues elsewhere. Before stopping the neighboring-average equality makes V of the walk a bounded martingale; the stopping time is bounded by τB​. Applying the bounded stopping identity by first truncating the time and then passing to the limit proves the expected terminal reward equals V(i).
Distinct rewards do not guarantee uniqueness. With N=2 and r(0)=0,r(1)=1,r(2)=2, the reward function is already linear and V=r. From state one, stopping gives one, while continuing to the next step also gives expected reward (0+2)/2=1. Both policies are optimal. Thus the claimed uniqueness is false even when all rewards are distinct.

(127)
Substitution gives Rabcd​(0)=4(ηac​ηbd​−ηad​ηbc​)/L2. In four dimensions the indicated contraction is
R(0)=L24​(42−4)=L248​.​
(128)
The sign is fixed by the Riemann-tensor formula in the question; reversing the Riemann convention would reverse the scalar as well.

In the thin-current approximation, vertical momentum balance is hydrostatic: p=patm​+ρg(h−z). Neglect inertia and radial viscous derivatives compared with the vertical ones. The radial Stokes equation is μuzz​=pr​=ρghr​, with no slip at z=0 and zero tangential stress uz​=0 at z=h. Integration gives
u(r,z,t)=−μρg​hr​(hz−2z2​).​
(129)
Its depth-integrated radial flux is Qr​=∫0h​udz=−ρgh3hr​/(3μ). Axisymmetric mass conservation ht​+r−1∂r​(rQr​)=0 therefore gives
ht​=rβ​∂r​(rh3hr​),β=3μρg​.​
(130)
The remaining conditions are conserved volume 2π∫0R(t)​rhdr=V, regularity and zero radial flux at the center, h(R(t),t)=0, zero thickness outside the front, and the initially concentrated volume at the origin. The advancing edge obeys R′=limr↑R​Qr​/h when this limit exists. One must not impose a finite zero slope at this compact-support edge.
Put h=taF(rt−b) with dimensional factors to be restored. Constant volume gives a+2b=0, while balancing the equation gives a−1=4a−2b. Hence a=−1/4,b=1/8. In normalized similarity variables η=r/(βV3t)1/8 and h=V1/4(βt)−1/4F(η), the equation becomes
−41​F−81​ηF′=η1​(ηF3F′)′.
(131)
Multiplying by η and integrating from the regular center yields ηF3F′=−η2F/8. Where F>0, this integrates to F3=3(η02​−η2)/16. Restoring physical variables gives
h(r,t)=[16βt3​(R(t)2−r2)]1/3(0≤r≤R(t)),​
(132)
with zero thickness outside. Write h=A(t)(1−r2/R2)1/3. Its volume is 3πAR2/4, so A=4V/(3πR2). Combining this with A3=3R2/(16βt) gives
R(t)=(81π31024βV3t​)1/8.​
(133)
The center height scales as t−1/4, while the front scales as t1/8. The ideal profile has a singular slope at the edge; microscopic contact-line physics is excluded from the lubrication model, which applies to the sufficiently spread bulk current.

For a one-dimensional isentropic perfect gas, continuity and momentum are Dρ=−ρux​ and Du=−c2ρx​/ρ, where D=∂t​+u∂x​ and c2=∂P/∂ρ. Since P=Kργ, differentiation gives
Dc=−2γ−1​cux​,Du=−γ−12c​cx​.
(134)
Thus applying D+c∂x​ to u+2(c−c0​)/(γ−1) cancels both terms:
(∂t​+(u+c)∂x​)[u+γ−12(c−c0​)​]=0.​
(135)
The complementary invariant u−2(c−c0​)/(γ−1) is transported along dx/dt=u−c. In the right-running piston simple wave, those characteristics carry the undisturbed value zero, giving c=c0​+(γ−1)u/2.
A right-running characteristic emitted by the piston at time τ has u=fτ and speed u+c=c0​+(γ+1)fτ/2, constant along that characteristic. It starts at x=fτ2/2, so
x(t;τ)=21​fτ2+(c0​+2γ+1​fτ)(t−τ).
(136)
Neighboring characteristics first intersect when ∂x/∂τ=0. This derivative is 2γ+1​ft−c0​−γfτ, so the envelope time is
t(τ)=(γ+1)f2c0​​+γ+12γ​τ.
(137)
For γ>1, it is smallest at τ=0. Consequently the first gradient catastrophe and ensuing shock form at
t∗​=(γ+1)f2c0​​,x∗​=c0​t∗​=(γ+1)f2c02​​.​
(138)
This uses the smooth isentropic simple-wave solution up to its first characteristic crossing, not beyond the newly formed shock.

38A OurBigBook.com
For a finite-dimensional linear operator A, the Krylov subspace is
Km​(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Am−1v}.
(139)
These spaces are nested, so their dimensions are nondecreasing and can rise by at most one at each step. If v=0, let k be the first index for which Akv is a linear combination of v,…,Ak−1v. The preceding k vectors are independent. Multiplying that dependence by A and repeatedly substituting shows every higher power also lies in their span. Thus
dm​=m (1≤m≤k),dm​=k (m≥k).​
(140)
Such an index exists because the ambient space is finite-dimensional. If v=0, the separate answer is dm​=0 for every m, with k=0.
For Krylov dimension from spectral components, when A is diagonalizable, group the eigenvector expansion by distinct eigenvalues:
v=u1​+⋯+uk​,Auj​=λj​uj​,
(141)
where each uj​ is its nonzero component in a distinct eigenspace. Then Arv=∑j​λjr​uj​. The vectors uj​ are independent, and the Vandermonde matrix (λjr​)0≤r<k​ is invertible because the eigenvalues are distinct. Hence the first k powers span exactly span{uj​}, proving the stabilized dimension equals the number of distinct eigenspaces with nonzero component in v. These uj​ themselves are eigenvectors, so this is also the minimum number of eigenvectors needed to represent v when the eigenvectors may be chosen freely.
If the printed phrase instead means the count of nonzero coefficients in an arbitrary fixed eigenbasis, it is false with repeated eigenvalues. For example A=I and v=e1​+e2​ use two vectors of that basis but have dimKm​=1; the vector v itself is an eigenvector. For a simple spectrum there is no distinction. This qualification resolves the claim without assuming an unstated simple spectrum.
